units.title: Quadratic variation of a finite predictable diffusion row
units.statement: The compensated sum of the squares of actual diffusion-row increments is in L² on each dyadic grid and converges to zero in mean square.
assumptions: All coordinates are from one Euclidean Brownian driver with the stated filtration.
Every row coefficient is strongly measurable at its cell’s left endpoint, in L⁴, and subject to one uniform fourth-moment bound.
The coordinate type is finite. The horizon may be zero.

proof.title: Control the product weights
proof.text: The average of two fourth powers bounds the square of the product. This gives the L² domain and the required uniform second moments.

proof.title: Apply the diagonal and mixed results
proof.text: The diagonal subtracts the elapsed time; distinct coordinates use the actual mixed increment product.

proof.title: Expand the actual row square
proof.text: Expanding the square and the compensator gives the finite sum over all ordered coordinate pairs.

proof.title: Transfer the finite-sum limit
proof.text: Each pair sum is square integrable and its squared expectation tends to zero. The square of the whole sum is bounded by the number of pairs times the sum of squares.

units.boundary: The coefficients are the specified grid rows. A continuous approximation has separate integrability and convergence obligations.

units.title: A coordinate column of the sphere projection formula
units.statement: For any j in I and any ambient vector x, take the j-th coordinate vector and subtract x_j times x.
assumptions: I is a finite coordinate type with decidable equality. The space is real Euclidean space on I.
The coordinate j belongs to I and x is any ambient vector.

proof.title: Apply the rank-one formula to one coordinate
proof.text: The inner product of x with the coordinate vector e_j is x_j. This is the action of the matrix I−xxᵀ on e_j.

units.boundary: The definition alone is a coordinate formula. The separately proved inner-product identity shows tangency on the unit sphere in the finite-dimensional setting.

units.title: The algebraic sphere-generator identity
units.statement: Fix a unit vector \(w\in\mathbb R^I\), a real function \(f\), an ambient vector \(u\), and \(\lambda\ge0\). Interpret \(Df\) and \(D^2f\) as the total Fréchet-derivative operators used in Lean. With projected columns \(p_j=e_j-w_jw\), the displayed algebraic equality holds. For a C² ambient test near the unit sphere, it is the usual identity for the Itô generator with noise columns \(\sqrt{2\lambda}\,p_j\) and radial drift \(-\lambda(d-1)w\), where \(d=|I|\).
assumptions: The coordinate set is finite with decidable equality, $\|w\|=1$, and $\lambda\ge 0$.

The vector \(u\) is arbitrary. No smoothness hypothesis is needed for the total-derivative algebra equality. The interpretation as a classical generator requires a C² ambient test; when \(u\) is also tangent, its first-order term is the directional derivative of the restricted test.
The operators are total: Lean assigns zero to a Fréchet derivative where differentiability fails. The classical derivative interpretation is only asserted under the smooth-test qualification above.

proof.title: Remove the noise amplitude from the trace
proof.text: The Hessian is bilinear and the square root is taken of a nonnegative number. Squaring the amplitude and multiplying by one half gives the temperature.

proof.title: Combine the radial drift and Hessian
proof.text: The projected trace removes one radial Hessian entry. The radial drift gives the first-derivative term with factor $d-1$.

units.boundary: The result is a pointwise identity for total derivative operators at one unit state, including temperature zero. Its classical generator interpretation uses the downstream C² test assumptions; its restricted directional-derivative interpretation also uses tangent u.

units.title: The exact mean-square error for predictable Brownian weights
units.statement: Let aᵢ be square-integrable real weights measurable at the left endpoints of a nondecreasing finite deterministic time grid. For Brownian motion B relative to that filtration, the compensated weighted square-increment sum is square-integrable and satisfies the exact identity below.
assumptions: B is a real Brownian motion with the given filtration and measure; its law implies the measure is a probability measure. There are n≥0 cells with 0≤t₀≤⋯≤tₙ.
For every cell i, aᵢ is strongly measurable with respect to the filtration at tᵢ and belongs to L². Repeated times are allowed.
units.formula: Z=\sum_i a_i\big((B_{t_{i+1}}-B_{t_i})^2-\Delta t_i\big),\qquad \mathbb E Z^2=2\sum_i\mathbb E[a_i^2](\Delta t_i)^2.

proof.title: Factor the diagonal second moments
proof.text: The compensated square of one increment has mean zero and second moment 2(Δt)². It is independent of every left-endpoint measurable weight. This also proves L² integrability of each weighted term.

proof.title: Eliminate the off-diagonal terms
proof.text: For i<j, the earlier weighted increment and the j-th weight are measurable at tⱼ. The j-th centered increment is independent of their product and has mean zero.

proof.title: Expand the square and retain only the diagonal
proof.text: Each product is integrable by the L² bounds. Interchange finite sums and integrals, cancel the cross terms and substitute the diagonal moments.

units.boundary: Weights need no almost-sure uniform bound. They may be dependent across cells; the required condition is left-endpoint measurability and a finite second moment.

units.title: The chosen representative is measurable
units.statement: If E is a measurable space and K is measurable, the map r:E→K is measurable for the induced subtype measurable structure.
assumptions: E is a type, K⊆E, and k₀ is a specified member of K. The result does not assume compactness.
E has a measurable structure and K is a measurable set.

proof.title: Express the underlying map as a measurable piecewise map
proof.text: The identity and the constant k₀ are measurable. Their piecewise combination on K is measurable, and the same map lifts to the subtype.

units.boundary: No topology, compactness or continuity of r is asserted.

units.title: Coordinate quadratic variation controls the vector Taylor residual
units.statement: In a finite-dimensional Euclidean state space, it suffices that the square-increment sum of each coordinate converge in measure to its own real-valued Qⱼ. The vector Taylor residual sum then converges in measure to zero.
assumptions: I is a finite coordinate set, E=ℝᴵ with its Euclidean norm, Ω carries a finite measure μ, and K⊆E is compact.
f:E→ℝ is C² at every point of K. The K-valued process X has measurable evaluations at every nonnegative time and almost-sure continuous paths on [0,T], where T>0.
For each j∈I the dyadic square-increment sum of coordinate j converges in measure to Qⱼ:Ω→ℝ.

proof.title: Sum the coordinate limits
proof.text: Coordinate increments are measurable. A finite simultaneous subsequence argument allows their convergence-in-measure limits to be summed.

proof.title: Recognize the Euclidean square norm
proof.text: Interchange the two finite sums and use the Euclidean norm identity. This supplies the square-increment hypothesis of the dyadic residual theorem.

units.boundary: The coordinate variation limits are inputs here. The result includes any finite coordinate set and claims convergence in measure, not pathwise convergence of the original sequence.
